en: The Scripture on Mañjuśrī’s Perambulation, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
Therein, he was together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, during the late afternoon, the World-Honored One emerged from his own chamber and sat in a spacious area outside, surrounded by the great assembly who paid him respectful homage and made offerings, while he preached the Dharma for them.

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, wandering in succession through all the places where those five hundred bhikṣus dwelt and stayed, eventually arrived at the place of the elder Śāriputra. He saw the elder Śāriputra sitting alone in one spot with his body erect, having entered meditative concentration in contemplation.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, having seen the elder Śāriputra, spoke to him, saying: "Venerable Śāriputra!
“Have you entered meditative concentration? The Elder Śāriputra replied, “It is so, Mañjuśrī!”
Mañjuśrī said, "Venerable Śāriputra, do you enter meditative absorption because you are not yet tranquil and wish to become tranquil?"
"Prior to this tranquility, what was it that was tranquil? Have you entered dhyāna, Venerable Śāriputra?
Upon what dhyāna do you rely?"
Do you enter meditative concentration by relying on the past, the future, the present, or the internal and external?
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
“Is it meditation based on the body, or is it meditation based on the mind?
The Venerable Śāriputra said, “Mañjuśrī!...”
"This meaning of my dhyāna is such that all those who dwell in the joyful practice of seeing the Dharma and all those whose minds are undistracted possess such right mindfulness.
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Śāriputra!"
Have you attained that Dharma?
What is that Dharma? Is it the Dharma of seeing which is pleasant to practice?
"Do you not see the practice of the joy of the Dharma? The Elder Śāriputra said, "Mañjuśrī!"
If one does not attain those dharmas, what dharma could there be?
If one sees the practice of delighting in dharmas, one does not see the practice of delighting in dharmas. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
"The Tathāgata has taught the Dharma for the abandonment of desire for those śrāvakas; I have entered into dhyāna by relying upon that Dharma. Mañjuśrī said:
"Venerable Śāriputra!..."
"What is this dharma of detachment that the Tathāgata taught for those śrāvakas, which the Venerable Śāriputra relies upon and practices?
The Elder Śāriputra replied, "Mañjuśrī!..."
In this way, a bhikṣu relies on past conduct, relies on future conduct, relies on present conduct, and so forth, up to relying on mental conduct; these matters should be understood accordingly.
Mañjuśrī! For the sake of those śrāvakas, the Tathāgata has taught this Dharma of detachment from desire; I follow that Dharma and practice in accordance with it.
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Śāriputra!
If you speak in this way—relying on past conduct, relying on future conduct, relying on present conduct, and even relying on the mind’s detachment from desire to act—and so forth."
Venerable Śāriputra!

If those dharmas did not exist for the Tathāgatas of the past, do not exist for the Tathāgatas of the future, and do not exist for the Tathāgatas of the present, then these dharmas are thus non-existent.
"Venerable Śāriputra!
Why do you now speak in this way:
'Relying on past formations, relying on future formations, relying on present formations'?"
Because there are no dharmas, there is likewise nothing upon which to rely.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra,
as for the Tathāgatas of the past, the future, and the present, there is no one who causes them to abide, nor is there any place where they might abide.
If there were no abiding, it could not be apprehended.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra,
if someone should say:
"To say that 'the Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present have a basis or are without basis'—
such a person slanders the Tathāgata. Why is this so?"
Suchness is without thought, nor is there anything to which it thinks.
Suchness does not regress; Suchness is without marks.
"Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra!

The suchness of the past is unapprehendable; the suchness of the future is unapprehendable; the suchness of the present is unapprehendable; and so on, up to the suchness of the mind, which is unapprehendable—all such things should be understood in this way.
"Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra,
there is no dharma whatsoever that exists outside of suchness (tathatā) which can be manifested or explained.
The Elder Śāriputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! After the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, have abided in suchness (tathatā), they then preach the Dharma. Mañjuśrī said:
"Venerable Śāriputra! Since true suchness (tathatā) does not exist, how could a Tathāgata, having dwelt in true suchness, preach the Dharma?
Venerable Śāriputra!"
Those dharmas also do not exist; how could the Tathāgata, having dwelt in suchness, preach the Dharma?
The Tathāgata also does not exist; where could the Tathāgata, having dwelt in suchness, preach the Dharma?
All phenomena are unattainable, and the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are likewise unattainable.
Furthermore, both these attainable and unattainable phenomena—these two kinds—are themselves unattainable.
The Tathāgata neither speaks nor does he not speak.
Why is this? Venerable Śāriputra!
“The Tathāgata has no speech, nor can he be described by words;
this is the Tathāgata. The Venerable Śāriputra said, “Mañjuśrī!...”
"Who, then, would receive such a Dharma?
Mañjuśrī replied, "Venerable Śāriputra!..."
If a person does not grasp at the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*) and does not long for nirvāṇa, such a person can receive this Dharma.

If a person does not apprehend past phenomena and does not know those phenomena, and does not apprehend future or present phenomena and does not know those phenomena, such a person can receive this Dharma.
If one does not perceive defilement, nor perceive purity; if one has no mind of grasping—such a person is able to receive this Dharma.
If it is neither the practice of self nor the practice of non-self, and neither the practice of grasping nor the practice of abandoning—such a person is able to receive this Dharma.
"Such a person as this can understand the meaning of what has been taught.
The Elder Śāriputra said, "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is it that is to be known? Mañjuśrī replied, "Venerable Śāriputra!"
"This is ineffable and there is nothing to be asked;
what is it that is known? The Elder Śāriputra said, "Mañjuśrī!"
The Dharma I preach is exceedingly profound; those who can believe in this Dharma are extremely few indeed. Mañjuśrī!
Even Arhats, as well as those in training and those beyond training, do not yet constitute its sphere of experience, let alone all ignorant ordinary beings.
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Śāriputra! So it is, so it is!"
Even the state of an Arhat is not their domain. Why is this?
An Arhat has no domains; an Arhat is called such because they have no abiding and no location.
It cannot be described; thus it is called "Arhat.
Because there is no description, it is called "Arhat. Why is this?
Being unconditioned and non-abiding is called being an arhat.
In what sphere does that arhat dwell?
An arhat is neither name nor form; it is only the deluded ordinary person who discriminates between name and form.
An Arhat is one who does not conceptually discriminate regarding name-and-form;
thus they are called an Arhat. An Arhat neither discriminates name nor discriminates form.
Foolish ordinary beings cannot be apprehended, nor can the dharmas of ordinary beings;
Arhats cannot be apprehended, nor can the dharmas of Arhats.

If it cannot be apprehended, then there is no conceptual differentiation; if there is no conceptual differentiation, then there is no activity; if there is no activity, then there is no proliferation; if there is no proliferation, this is tranquility. Thus, there is neither activity nor proliferation.
One who is tranquil does not grasp at existence, nor does he grasp at non-existence; being neither existent nor non-existent, he does not grasp in this manner.

If one does not grasp, then there is nothing to be attained. Such a person is free from all attainment; being without mind and detached from the mind, they abide in the Dharma of the Śrāvakas—thus should it be understood.
At that time, when the youth Mañjuśrī had finished preaching this Dharma, those five hundred bhikṣus rose from their seats and departed, saying:
"We have no need to see the body of the youth Mañjuśrī, nor do we have any need to hear the name of the youth Mañjuśrī."
In whatever place the youth Mañjuśrī may reside, that place should also be abandoned. Why is this?
Because such a youth Mañjuśrī’s holy life is different from mine; therefore, he should be shunned.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!
In explaining the meaning of this Dharma, do you not intend for all sentient beings to understand its meaning?”
Mañjuśrī said: "So it is, so it is! Venerable Śāriputra!"
The Elder Śāriputra said:
"How is it that these five hundred bhikṣus have risen from their seats and departed, disparaging, engaging in frivolous debate, and slandering [this teaching]?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Śāriputra! If these bhikṣus speak in this manner:..."
"I do not need this body of the youth Mañjuśrī, nor do I need to hear the name of the youth Mañjuśrī; in whatever place the youth Mañjuśrī may dwell, that place too should be abandoned."
"Excellent, excellent, Venerable Śāriputra! These bhikṣus have spoken these words well."
Why is this? Because Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta does not exist, he cannot be apprehended.

Since he is non-existent and cannot be apprehended, he cannot be seen nor can he be heard; furthermore, in whatever direction or location Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta might reside, that place too should be abandoned.
If it is spoken in this way, then even the dwelling place of the youth Mañjuśrī does not exist; if that does not exist, then it can neither be approached nor abandoned.

At that time, after the youth Mañjuśrī had spoken this Dharma, five hundred bhikṣus, having heard it, turned their faces away. Having turned their faces away, they then spoke these words to the youth Mañjuśrī:
“Mañjuśrī has spoken such a Dharma as this; we are not able to understand it.”
Mañjuśrī said: “Excellent, excellent!
You bhikṣus, as disciples of the Tathāgata and śrāvakas, should train yourselves in this way.”
"O bhikṣus! Such a Dharma as this is not known by consciousness, nor is it known by wisdom. Why is that?"
Because it is the very nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

The dharma-realm is thus without thought and without regression; just as that dharma is without thought and without regression, it is not known by consciousness (*vijñāna*), nor is it known by wisdom (*jñāna*).
"Whatever is not known by consciousness and not known by wisdom is not an object of mindfulness.
You, bhikṣus, who are śrāvakas and disciples of the Tathāgata, should train yourselves in this way."
"If one trains in this way, the Buddha says that such a person attains the most supreme Dharma; they are a field of merit for the world and should receive offerings.
When this Dharma was spoken, among those five hundred bhikṣus, four hundred bhikṣus did not grasp at any phenomena, exhausted all fetters and outflows, and their minds attained liberation;
one hundred bhikṣus gave rise to evil thoughts, and their own bodies were about to fall into the great hell.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī!
Your teaching of the Dharma does not protect sentient beings, for you have caused the loss of these one hundred bhikṣus."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Śāriputra, saying:
"You, Śāriputra, do not speak in such a manner. Why is this?

Śāriputra! These one hundred bhikṣus fell into the Great Howling Hell; yet, after experiencing a single touch, they were reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven in a place of common karma, because they had heard such a Dharma as this.
Śāriputra! If these bhikṣus do not hear such a Dharma-gate, they will certainly fall into hell.
Only after a kalpa has passed will they be born among human beings.
Because they have heard this Dharma-gate, the karma that would have caused them to fall into hell for one kalpa shall be reduced to a minor retribution. Śāriputra!
These hundred bhikṣus will become śrāvakas within the first assembly of the Tathāgata Maitreya, where they shall realize arhatship and exhaust all outflows.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
The merit obtained from hearing this Dharma-gate is superior; it is not equal to practicing the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the three samāpattis of the formless realm.
Why is this? If one does not hear this Dharma-gate, then one cannot be liberated from birth and death.
I say that such a person cannot be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, and death, nor from sorrow, suffering, grief, lamentation, and despair.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra said to the youth Mañjuśrī,
"It is truly rare, Mañjuśrī, that you are able so skillfully to expound such a Dharma-gate for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity."
Mañjuśrī said: "Venerable Śāriputra!
True suchness neither decreases nor increases; the dharma-realm neither decreases nor increases; and the realms of all sentient beings neither decrease nor increase."
Why is this? It is merely words;
there is no person upon whom to rely, and no place upon which to rely. It is neither reliance nor non-reliance.
Venerable Śāriputra!
Thus, non-reliance is itself bodhi; thus, bodhi is itself liberation.
If one relies on dharmas, that is conceptual discrimination;
if one knows that there is neither action nor non-action, that is nirvana.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Śāriputra, saying: "So it is, so it is! Śāriputra!"

As the youth Mañjuśrī has said: true thusness neither decreases nor increases; the dharma-realm neither decreases nor increases; and the realms of all sentient beings neither decrease nor increase, being neither defiled nor pure.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning, spoke again in verse:
"To speak of phenomena of the past, future, and present worlds—such verbal expression is not the ultimate meaning;
it is neither with characteristics nor without characteristics."
Whether characterized by marks or markless, there is nothing at all to be discriminated;
it is through discrimination that they are attained, and through discrimination they are markless.
If one discriminates conditioned phenomena, then one discriminates nirvana.
Both of these are the works of Māra; the wise know them thus.
The aggregates, sense-bases, and elements are mere names; they are neither arising nor ceasing, and are without marks.
If one observes and discriminates them, then one does not truly observe.
The wise do not engage in conceptual discrimination; they move through the sphere of experience as if it were empty space.
If one discriminates, one grasps; if one does not discriminate, one does not grasp.
Through discrimination and grasping, one is bound; through non-discrimination, one is liberated.
If one knows such dharmas as these, that person is called wise.
Such a person attains exhaustion [of suffering] and is named one of non-discriminative wisdom.
Because they possess wisdom, they are called "wise"; yet it is taught that both [wisdom and its object] are empty.
If a person understands in this way, that person is called wise.
Even the merit obtained from giving away treasures that fill the three thousandfold world-system is surpassed by the merit of one who hears this Dharma.
Practicing generosity, ethical discipline, and patience, with unimpeded supernormal powers,
one may constantly cultivate these for billions of eons, yet it would not equal hearing this sutra. If one knows this Dharma gate,
spoken by the One of Perfect and Universal Knowledge, [one attains the supreme fruit].
"Having heard this sutra, all shall become Tathāgatas.
After the Tathāgata had spoken this Dharma-gate, ten thousand sentient beings were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena;
five hundred bhikṣus resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One bestowed upon the five hundred bhikṣus the prediction of Buddhahood, speaking these words:
"O bhikṣus, during the Star Simile Kalpa, you shall all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; you shall all share the same name, namely, Dharmapadma Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha."

When the Blessed One had finished speaking, the youth Mañjuśrī, the elder Śāriputra, gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on Mañjuśrī’s Peripatetic Journey Spoken by the Buddha
